checks.name: DMARC
checks.explanation: Your DMARC policy is set to p=none (monitoring mode). The record is valid. p=none asks receivers to take no action on failing mail. It is the usual starting point for collecting aggregate reports. To stop spoofing, move to an enforcement policy (p=quarantine or p=reject) once your legitimate mail streams are aligned.

details.text: Policy p=none: monitoring only, no enforcement requested

checks.fix: Review your DMARC aggregate reports to identify all legitimate senders and confirm they pass SPF or DKIM with aligned domains. Once you are confident in your sender inventory, move to an enforcement policy (p=quarantine or p=reject).

checks.message: p=none is a valid policy value.

strict_validation.summary: This record passes RFC 9989 strict validation.

overall.label: Moderate Risk
overall.summary: This domain has multiple paths for email spoofing attacks.

vectors.name: Direct Domain Spoofing
vectors.summary: No DMARC action is requested for failing mail (p=none).
vectors.detail: An attacker could send an email appearing to be from ceo@ietf.org to your employees requesting a wire transfer. No DMARC action is requested, so each receiver applies only its own filtering to mail that fails.

vectors.name: Subdomain Spoofing
vectors.detail: An attacker could send from support@helpdesk.ietf.org to your customers requesting password resets. The subdomain looks legitimate but has no protection.

vectors.name: Non-Existent Subdomain Spoofing
vectors.detail: A subdomain that was never created, such as secure-portal.ietf.org, has no record of its own, so mail claiming to come from it is judged by the policy it inherits. Here that policy is not enforcing. RFC 9091 added the np tag for exactly this case.

vectors.name: Reporting Intelligence
vectors.detail: Aggregate reports are sent to verified destinations.

attack_surface.attacker_path: The easiest path to spoofing this domain is direct: mail sent as user@ietf.org is not blocked, because the policy is p=none.

health.label: Monitoring
health.summary: This domain is in monitoring mode and is not yet protected against spoofing. Review your reports and progress toward an enforcing policy.

tags.label: Version
tags.explanation: Valid DMARC version identifier. Required as the first tag.
tags.dmarcbis_note: Both RFC 7489 and RFC 9989 require v=DMARC1 to be the first tag. A record with it anywhere else is not a DMARC record.

tags.label: Policy
tags.explanation: Monitoring only. p=none requests no action, so each receiver applies only its own filtering to mail that fails. It is the right first step for collecting aggregate reports; the goal is to progress to p=quarantine and then p=reject once every legitimate sender aligns.

warnings.text: Monitoring only. No enforcement is applied to messages that fail authentication.

tags.dmarcbis_note: RFC 9989 clarifies policy semantics and removes ambiguities in how receivers interpret these values. The biggest change is replacing pct with the binary t=y test mode for safer policy rollout.

tags.label: Subdomain Policy
tags.explanation: Subdomains inherit the root policy (p=none). Setting sp= explicitly makes the record say what it means, so a later change to p= cannot loosen subdomains by accident.
tags.dmarcbis_note: RFC 9989 clarifies inheritance. sp covers subdomains that have no DMARC record of their own; np, imported from RFC 9091, lets non-existent subdomains carry a stricter policy than real ones.

tags.label: Non-Existent Subdomain Policy
tags.explanation: No non-existent subdomain policy. Falls back to sp= (if set), then p=. Current effective policy for non-existent subdomains: p=none.

warnings.text: Non-existent subdomains such as secure-login.ietf.org currently fall to p=none, so mail from an invented name is not rejected. Consider adding np=reject.

tags.dmarcbis_note: RFC 9989 brings np in from RFC 9091. Under RFC 7489 a subdomain that does not exist inherited sp, or p when sp was absent, so it could not be set separately. np lets you hold sp=none while a real subdomain is still being aligned and reject mail from names that were never created at the same time.

tags.label: DKIM Alignment Mode
tags.explanation: Defaults to relaxed (r). Subdomain alignment is permitted.
tags.dmarcbis_note: RFC 9989 clarifies alignment edge cases, especially around subdomains and how organizational domain is determined (now via tree walk instead of PSL).

tags.label: SPF Alignment Mode
tags.dmarcbis_note: RFC 9989 explicitly states that DMARC evaluates SPF against the MAIL FROM identity only, not HELO. RFC 7489 let receivers fall back to HELO when MAIL FROM was empty.

tags.label: Failure Reporting Options
tags.explanation: Defaults to fo=0. Reports only on complete failure of both mechanisms.
tags.dmarcbis_note: The fo tag is defined in RFC 9989 section 4.7, but the reports it governs are specified in RFC 9991. Most large receivers, Google and Microsoft among them, do not send failure reports at all.

tags.label: Aggregate Report Recipients
tags.explanation: Aggregate reports are sent to mailto:dmarc_agg@vali.email,mailto:dmarc-report@ietf.org. These show which sources send mail as your domain and whether they pass or fail authentication. Review before moving to enforcement.
tags.dmarcbis_note: Reporting moved into its own documents: RFC 9990 for aggregate reports and RFC 9991 for failure reports. The size suffix on a URI (such as !10m) was removed (RFC 9989 Appendix C.4). URI syntax is otherwise unchanged.

tags.label: Forensic Report Recipients
tags.explanation: No failure reporting. Common since most providers don't send them. Aggregate reports provide sufficient visibility.
tags.dmarcbis_note: Failure reporting is now defined in its own document, RFC 9991.

tags.label: Percentage
tags.explanation: Not in this record. RFC 9989 removed the tag.

tags.label: Report Format
tags.explanation: Not in this record. RFC 9989 removed the tag.

tags.label: Report Interval
tags.explanation: Not in this record. RFC 9989 removed the tag.

tags.label: Public Suffix Domain
tags.explanation: Not declared, which is the RFC 9989 default ('u') and correct for almost every domain. Receivers determine the organizational domain with the tree walk. Publish psd= only if this domain is a public suffix.
tags.dmarcbis_note: New in RFC 9989. It replaces the Public Suffix List, a file maintained outside DNS, for finding the organizational domain.

tags.label: Testing Mode
tags.explanation: Normal enforcement. Policies applied as published.
tags.dmarcbis_note: New in RFC 9989, replacing pct. Under RFC 7489, pct=50 meant 'apply to 50% of failing mail', but receivers implemented it inconsistently. Only pct=0 and pct=100 were reliable. t=y asks receivers to apply one level below the published policy. t=n, or no t tag, applies it in full.

config_warnings.title: Monitoring mode
config_warnings.text: Monitoring mode. Review your aggregate reports and progress to p=quarantine then p=reject once every legitimate sender aligns.

config_warnings.title: SPF alignment under RFC 9989
config_warnings.text: Under RFC 9989, SPF alignment is evaluated against the MAIL FROM (envelope sender) identity only, not HELO.

config_warnings.title: RFC 9989 reporting restructured
config_warnings.text: RFC 9989 splits the specification into three separate RFCs: core mechanism, aggregate reporting, and failure reporting.

config_warnings.title: External reporting destinations
config_warnings.text: Aggregate reports are sent to domains: ietf.org, vali.email.

steps.action: Review aggregate reports until the sender inventory is stable
steps.why: Identify every legitimate sender and fix their SPF or DKIM alignment before enforcing. Move on when a full reporting cycle shows no new legitimate sources, not on a date.

t=y asks RFC 9989 receivers to apply one level below the published policy, so they treat p=quarantine; t=y as p=none. Receivers still on RFC 7489 ignore t and quarantine in full. Publish this step only when your reports already show no legitimate failures.
Once reports show no legitimate mail failures, enforce quarantine.

t=y asks RFC 9989 receivers to apply one level below the published policy, so they treat p=reject; t=y as p=quarantine. Receivers still on RFC 7489 ignore t and reject in full. Publish this step only when quarantine has run with no legitimate failures.
Full protection. Mail failing authentication is blocked.

steps.action: Make subdomain policy explicit: sp=reject, np=reject
steps.why: Neither changes what receivers do here, since both already inherit reject. They make the record say what it means, so a later change to p= cannot loosen subdomains by accident.

changes.reason: Enforce reject to block spoofed mail. Use t=y if you need a testing period first.
Makes the subdomain policy explicit; it already inherits the root policy.
Makes the non-existent subdomain policy explicit; the tag comes from RFC 9091.

deploy.note_ttl: Changes typically propagate within minutes, depending on your DNS provider's TTL.

sections.title: What is RFC 9989 (DMARCbis)?
sections.content: RFC 9989 is the DMARC standard. Published in May 2026 on the IETF Standards Track, it replaces RFC 7489 and RFC 9091, the documents that defined DMARC until then. It is still widely called DMARCbis, the name it carried through the working group. It addresses real-world problems discovered over a decade of DMARC deployment: inconsistent parsing across receivers, unreliable percentage-based rollout, no protection for non-existent subdomains, and dependence on the manually-maintained Public Suffix List.

sections.title: What changed from RFC 7489?
items: Your record doesn't have an np= tag. np, brought into RFC 9989 from RFC 9091, sets a policy for subdomains that were never created. Under RFC 7489 they inherited sp, or p when sp was absent, so the two could not be set separately.
RFC 9989 defines the record grammar more strictly. A report address without mailto:, a duplicated tag, an empty value or a malformed URI that older tools accepted is now invalid.
RFC 9989 replaces the Public Suffix List with a DNS tree walk, capped at 8 queries, and adds the psd= tag so a domain can declare its own status.
RFC 9989 splits the specification into three separate RFCs: the core mechanism, aggregate reporting, and failure reporting.

sections.title: Where does this record stand?
sections.content: This scale reflects how completely the record matches RFC 9989, the current DMARC standard. Ready means it uses the current tags and needs no changes. Compatible means it works but leaves protection unused. Anything below that has gaps worth closing. This record is currently rated 'monitoring'.

sections.title: Why does this matter?
sections.content: When your domain can be spoofed, someone else can send phishing and fraud that appears to come from you. Your customers, partners, and employees see your name on it. The recipients who trusted it are harmed, and so is their trust in your real mail. RFC 9989 closes gaps RFC 7489 left open, particularly around non-existent subdomains and inconsistent receiver behavior.

sections.title: What should I do?
sections.content: See your personalized migration path above for step-by-step instructions to reach RFC 9989 Ready status.

checklist.label: np policy defined (non-existent domains)
checklist.np_fallback_note: Non-existent subdomains currently fall back to p=none
checklist.recommendation: Editorial recommendation (not spec-required): consider np=quarantine to flag mail from non-existent subdomains even while you keep p=none for monitoring. RFC 9989 section 4.7 does not prescribe an np value; if np is absent, the fallback is sp then p.

checklist.label: PSD indicator declared
checklist.note: Optional. RFC 9989 4.7 defaults psd= to 'u'. Publish it only if this domain is a public suffix.

changes.reason: Editorial suggestion (not spec-required): added np from p value to make non-existent subdomain policy explicit. RFC 9989 section 4.7 does not require this.

recommendations.recommendation: Editorial recommendation (not spec-required): consider np=quarantine to flag mail from non-existent subdomains even while you keep p=none for monitoring. RFC 9989 section 4.7 does not prescribe an np value; if np is absent, the fallback is sp then p.

checks.deliverability: With p=none, receivers apply their own filtering to mail that fails. Google, Yahoo, and Microsoft (Outlook.com) require a DMARC record from bulk senders, and p=none satisfies that requirement.
checks.what_this_is: Tells mail servers that receive your mail what to do with a message that claims to be from your domain but fails authentication. Without it, every receiver decides on its own, and you get no report of who is sending as you.

checks.name: MX Records
checks.explanation: Only one MX record is configured.

details.text: If this host becomes unavailable, inbound mail queues at the sending server and may eventually bounce.

checks.fix: Add a secondary MX record for failover.

ttl_info.label: Very short TTL
ttl_info.detail: Resolvers pick up a change to this record within 5 minutes.

checks.deliverability: You have only one mail server. If it goes down, incoming emails will queue at the sender's server for hours or days, and some senders give up after a few retries. A second MX host provides failover for incoming mail.
checks.what_this_is: The servers that accept mail addressed to your domain. Mail to you is delivered to whatever these name, in priority order.

checks.name: DKIM
checks.verdict: 1 DKIM public key published in DNS
checks.explanation: Found 1 live DKIM public key published in DNS. Each key is a TXT record at selector._domainkey.ietf.org. Receiving servers retrieve this key to verify the DKIM signature on incoming messages (RFC 6376). Note: this audit confirms the public key exists in DNS; it does not test live message signatures. Selectors were targeted using SPF-based sender discovery.

details.business_risk: This key is below the RSA size RFC 8301 recommends and should be rotated to a 2048-bit RSA key.

checks.fix: The following selectors use RSA keys below the recommended 2048 bits: mail (1024-bit). Key rotation is provider-specific. Check your email provider's documentation for how to generate and publish a new 2048-bit RSA key pair.

keys.rating_label: Weak by modern standards. NIST deprecated 1024-bit RSA in 2013. Rotate to 2048-bit.

dkim_deep.rotation_guidance: Rotate mail to 2048-bit. Steps: 1) Generate new key pair, 2) Publish new public key under new selector, 3) Configure mail server to sign with new selector, 4) After a few days, once mail signed with the old key has been delivered, empty its p= to revoke it.

checks.deliverability: This key (1024-bit) still verifies today. Rotate to 2048-bit before receivers stop accepting it.
checks.what_this_is: A signature added to every message you send, checked against a key you publish in DNS. It proves the message came from your domain and was not altered on the way.

checks.name: SPF
checks.explanation: SPF record ends with ~all (softfail): servers not listed here are not authorized to send mail for this domain. The SPF result feeds DMARC, and the DMARC policy decides what happens to mail that fails. With DMARC in place, ~all and -all are both sound choices.

details.text: ~all (softfail): servers not listed are not authorized

spf_deep.all_explanation: Servers not listed are not authorized. Receivers treat a softfail as a signal and leave the outcome to DMARC.
spf_deep.dmarcbis_note: Under RFC 9989, SPF alignment is evaluated against the MAIL FROM (envelope sender) identity only, not HELO. SPF pass alone does not guarantee DMARC pass. The MAIL FROM domain must also align with the From header domain.

checks.what_this_is: A DNS record listing the servers allowed to send mail for your domain. A receiver compares the server that delivered a message against that list.

checks.name: MTA-STS
checks.explanation: While DMARC protects the identity of the sender, MTA-STS (RFC 8461) protects the connection. It prevents downgrade attacks where a network attacker forces email to be delivered without encryption. Without MTA-STS, a sending server that cannot reach your mail server over TLS falls back to plaintext and nothing tells you.
checks.fix: MTA-STS requires a DNS TXT record at _mta-sts.ietf.org and a policy file hosted at https://mta-sts.ietf.org/.well-known/mta-sts.txt. The policy file specifies your MX hosts and the TLS enforcement mode.
checks.deliverability: MTA-STS covers mail sent to you. It has no effect on how your outgoing mail is filtered.
checks.what_this_is: A policy you publish telling sending servers to require TLS when they deliver to you, and to give up rather than fall back to plaintext. Without it, an attacker on the network can strip the encryption and read the mail.

checks.name: TLS-RPT
checks.explanation: Without TLS-RPT (RFC 8460), you have no visibility into encryption failures on inbound email delivery. If a sending server cannot establish a secure connection with your mail server, it may fall back to plaintext delivery or fail silently. TLS-RPT provides daily reports on these failures, allowing you to identify certificate issues or misconfigurations before they affect delivery.
checks.fix: Publish a TLS-RPT TXT record at _smtp._tls.ietf.org. Requires a reporting address (rua=) that can receive JSON-formatted TLS failure reports: either your own mailbox or a reporting service.
checks.what_this_is: An address you publish so senders can report failed TLS connections to your mail servers. It is how you find out that delivery is being downgraded or blocked.

checks.name: BIMI
checks.explanation: BIMI record is published. BIMI is a brand recognition feature, not a security protocol. Your brand logo URL is configured. Note: No certificate is referenced in the a= tag. Gmail requires a certificate in the a= tag: a VMC, which needs a registered trademark, or a CMC, which needs proof the logo has been in use for at least a year. Yahoo Mail can display the logo without one. Apple Mail requires a VMC.

details.text: The SVG declares the correct profile for BIMI.
The viewBox attribute is needed for proper scaling.

checks.fix: Move DMARC to p=quarantine or p=reject.
checks.what_this_is: Shows your logo beside your mail in the clients that support it. It is branding, not security, and it requires DMARC at quarantine or reject first.

checks.name: DNSSEC
checks.explanation: DNSSEC is enabled. Your DNS records are cryptographically signed per RFC 4033/4034/4035, allowing validating resolvers to confirm that responses have not been tampered with. This prevents cache poisoning and DNS spoofing, and is required for DANE to function.

details.text: DS record present at parent (chain of trust anchored)
DS digest matches DNSKEY (chain of trust verified)

checks.what_this_is: Signs your DNS records so a resolver can tell the answer it got is the answer you published. It stops an attacker from forging DNS answers for your domain, and it is what DANE is built on.

checks.name: CAA
checks.explanation: CAA records (RFC 8659) specify which Certificate Authorities are authorized to issue TLS certificates for your domain. Compliant CAs must check CAA records before issuance.

details.text: Neither this domain nor any parent up to the registrable domain publishes CAA records, so any Certificate Authority in the world can issue TLS certificates for your domain. CAA lets you restrict issuance to only the CAs you actually use, reducing the risk of unauthorized certificates.

checks.fix: Publish CAA records specifying which Certificate Authorities may issue certificates for your domain. Requires knowing which CAs you use. Use issue to authorize your CA, issuewild for wildcard policy, and iodef to receive violation alerts.
checks.what_this_is: A DNS record naming which certificate authorities may issue certificates for your domain. It does not affect mail; it limits who can get a certificate in your name.

checks.name: Nameservers
checks.explanation: Found 2 nameservers for this domain. Nameservers are authoritative for your DNS zone. They answer queries for all your DNS records. Multiple nameservers on distinct network paths reduce the risk of a single point of failure causing a full DNS outage for your domain.

details.text: This audit does not check blocklist listings. Blocklist operators refuse queries from cloud-hosted resolvers, so the answer would not be reliable. Check yours at check.spamhaus.org
All nameservers are hosted by Cloudflare. While this provider likely has internal redundancy, using a secondary DNS provider eliminates the risk of a provider-wide outage affecting your domain.

checks.what_this_is: The servers that answer every DNS question about your domain, including the records on this page. If they disagree with each other or stop answering, your mail and your website stop resolving.

checks.name: DANE
checks.explanation: DANE (RFC 7672) is configured: the TLSA records at each MX host validate under DNSSEC in that host's zone. Sending mail servers that implement RFC 7672 can verify your mail server's TLS certificate through those records, independent of the public CA trust model.

details.text: All 1 MX host have TLSA records
This domain's MX records are DNSSEC-signed, so they cannot be forged to redirect mail

checks.what_this_is: Publishes your mail server's certificate fingerprint in DNSSEC-signed DNS, so a sending server can verify the certificate without trusting a certificate authority. It requires DNSSEC on your zone and it fails closed, so mail stops if the record and the certificate drift apart.

checks.name: Certificate Transparency
checks.explanation: Certificate Transparency was not assessed. This audit reads CT data from the public crt.sh service, which did not answer within five seconds. That is common for domains with thousands of certificates and says nothing about your certificates either way. To review them yourself, search this domain on crt.sh.

details.text: crt.sh did not answer in time. This is a gap in the audit, not a finding about your domain.

checks.what_this_is: Public logs that every certificate authority writes to when it issues a certificate. Reading them shows every certificate that exists for your domain, including ones nobody at your company ordered.

anomalies.title: BIMI record without DMARC enforcement
anomalies.description: A BIMI record is published but DMARC policy is "none", not quarantine or reject. Mail clients will not display the BIMI logo because DMARC enforcement is required.
anomalies.recommendation: Set DMARC policy to at least quarantine (p=quarantine) before expecting mail clients to honour the BIMI logo.

guidance.text: Google Workspace supports 2048-bit DKIM. Enable in Admin Console > Apps > Google Workspace > Gmail > Authenticate Email.
Google's rollout guide starts at p=none with rua= and moves up only after the reports show every legitimate sender aligning.
Google rewrites the envelope sender for forwarded mail, which can break SPF alignment. DKIM is the more reliable alignment mechanism.

dmarc_eval.explanation: SPF and DKIM are configured with relaxed alignment, providing redundant paths to DMARC pass. Based on DNS records only, not live mail testing.

resilience.summary: DMARC is p=none (monitoring only). SPF and DKIM may be present, but receivers will not act on authentication failures. p=none requests no action, so each receiver applies only its own filtering to mail that fails.

spf.note: SPF record is valid (2/10 lookups used). SPF verifies that the sending server's IP address is authorized by the domain owner. However, SPF breaks when mail is forwarded because the forwarding server's IP is not in the original domain's SPF record.

dkim.note: DKIM key detected. DKIM signs each message with a cryptographic signature that travels with the email. Unlike SPF, DKIM survives forwarding because the signature is attached to the message itself, not tied to the sending server's IP. Selectors found: mail.

dmarc.note: DMARC policy is p=none (monitoring only). p=none requests no action, so each receiver applies only its own filtering to mail that fails. This is useful for collecting aggregate reports before enforcing, but provides no protection against spoofing.

resilience.risk: p=none is the right starting point for collecting data, but it provides no protection. Review DMARC aggregate reports (rua=) to identify all legitimate mail sources, ensure each one passes SPF or DKIM with alignment, and then move to p=quarantine. After confirming no legitimate mail is being caught, upgrade to p=reject.

items.impact: Nothing is blocked yet, and every receiver is making its own call on mail that fails.

items.action: Rotate the weak DKIM key to 2048-bit
items.impact: This key is below current recommendations and should be rotated.
Without MTA-STS, a sending server that cannot reach your mail server over TLS falls back to plaintext and nothing tells you.
You get no report when a sending server fails to reach your mail server over TLS.

items.action: Move DMARC to p=quarantine or p=reject.
items.impact: An issue with your existing BIMI setup may prevent your logo from displaying.

items.action: Add a secondary MX record for failover.

executive_summary.verdict: Your domain is monitoring email authentication but not yet enforcing it. This requests no action from receivers, who each decide independently what to do with mail that fails.
executive_summary.biggest_risk_detail: Nothing is blocked yet, and every receiver is making its own call on mail that fails.
executive_summary.deliverability_summary: Your DMARC policy is monitoring only (p=none). It provides visibility, not protection, until you move to p=quarantine or p=reject.
